newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - Brit Steel to pay job-loss price of stg.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Brit Steel to pay job-loss price of stg.

text.p: British Steel Plc, bracing itself to pay the price of a strong pound, confirmed on Thursday it planned to axe "significantly more" than 5,000 jobs in the next five years at a cost of "tens of millions of pounds".
The steel giant, one of the most efficient in Europe, is due to meet trade unions on Friday to discuss the plans and changes to working practices.

The news comes at a time when German steelworkers have taken to the streets to protest against Krupp's proposed hostile bid for rival Thyssen. The two German companies are now discussing cooperation which would avoid a takeover battle.
A British Steel spokesman said the pound's rise against the mark was the primary reason for the job cutting programme, but also blamed competition and overcapacity in the market.
The spokesman told Reuters there will be no plant closures, but that each group division will be instructed to go back and scale down operations in order to make them viable.

Brian Moffat, chairman and chief executive of British Steel, said to unions in a letter obtained by Reuters that the group was threatened by rate volatility, more competition in Europe and low-cost producers in Eastern Europe.

"The company will have to man and organise its facilities and business processes in increasingly imaginative ways, with fewer employees than now and a clear focus on our core activities," he said, adding that restrictive work practices and employment conditions would have to go.

Bob Shannon of the Amalgamated Engineering and Electrical Union told Reuters he had no job loss figures yet and added that the unions were not primed for industrial action at this stage. British Steel has already shed nearly 15,000 jobs since the early 1980s.

"We have been crucified by sterling," said Shannon. "This is no scare story. It is real. British Steel is already the most efficient steel company in Europe, so if sterling is hurting, you get an idea of how big a problem this is."

The British Steel spokesman said of the job cuts: "We are not putting a figure on it tomorrow. But since privatisation we have cut up to 1,000 jobs each year. We are now talking of significantly more than that over the next five years."
Asked to quantify the cost, he said it would be "Not hundreds of millions (of pounds) but tens of millions," and was unlikely to breach 100 million.
Eighty percent of British Steel's eight billion of sales is mark-sensitive. On the impact of the pound's surge, British Steel's spokesman said:

"It was at 2.25 marks for a long time and helped us make profits of 1.1 billion (pounds). Since then it has gone up as high as 2.75 and for every 10 pfennigs the pound gains, our profits drop by 100 million."
British Steel boss Moffat first warned last November that the pound could have a crippling effect.
That triggered wave after wave of profit forecast downgrades by analysts.
In the year to March 30 1996, British Steel's profits were 1.1 billion sterling, up 86 percent on 1995 at a time when the world industry was suffering from de-stocking and tough competition.

But the pound means analysts now expect profits of around 500 million sterling for the year ending March 31 97, a slump of 55 percent, and an even lower 325 million in profit for the year ending March 31 1998, a further fall of 35 percent.
Andy Chambers, analyst at SocGen, said the job cuts were in line with expectations.
He added British Steel was already very efficient, outstripping German rivals. Union leaders say they are willing to talk on improving performances further.
On how far unions are prepared to co-operate , Shannon said "That depends on the options put forward. But no-one is going to vote for something that makes their job disappear."
Concern over the company's profits dragged the British Steel price down from around 200 pence last year to a low of 139 earlier this year. It has since recovered to trade around around 159 pence.
($ = 0.624 British Pounds)
